task_row_model.query: How did Prussian military reforms between 1807 and 1815 change officer recruitment and the social composition of the officer corps?

documents.content: After Prussia's defeat in 1806 a wave of administrative and military reform was initiated, of which Gerhard von Scharnhorst was a leading architect. Between 1807 and 1814 the reforms established systematic officer education, created new training institutions for junior officers and non-commissioned officers, and instituted rules enabling promotion on merit rather than purely by birth. An 1808 regulation explicitly permitted capable lower-rank soldiers and qualified commoners to receive commissions, while organizational changes introduced the Landwehr as a reserve force drawn broadly from the population. The rhetoric of the reformers emphasized technical competence, literacy, and battlefield performance as criteria for advancement, and the reforms sought to widen the social base of the officer corps beyond the traditional aristocracy.
documents.reasoning_trace: Document provides core reform actions: dates, Scharnhorst role, officer schools, Landwehr creation, and merit-based promotion allowing non-nobles into commissions.

documents.content: Contemporary reports and later statistical summaries show a noticeable shift in the composition of Prussian officers during the Napoleonic wars and the immediate postwar period. Before 1807 about 85% of commissioned officers came from the nobility; by 1815 that proportion had fallen to roughly 60%. The gap was filled mainly by middle-class recruits—professionals, merchants and artisans—who rose to about 30% of officers, while those of peasant or commoner origin increased from approximately 5% to near 10%. Historians attribute this change to the combined effect of universal conscription into the Landwehr, which brought bourgeois volunteers into leadership roles, and to wartime merit promotions in 1813–1814 that rewarded competence over lineage.
documents.reasoning_trace: Document supplies quantifiable social-composition data and links the numeric shifts to conscription and wartime merit promotions.

documents.content: A veteran's memoir and several provincial correspondence pieces reflect the uneven reception and implementation of reforms. Local gentry in many districts resisted opening commissions, and some elite formations—most notably the Royal Guard regiments and select cavalry squadrons—retained a strong aristocratic character through patronage and tradition. Correspondents complained that while line infantry and Landwehr units quickly integrated officers from artisan and bourgeois backgrounds during the 1813 mobilization, the higher-status regiments preserved social exclusivity longer. These accounts are written in an anecdotal, argumentative style and include tangential reflections on court culture, provincial rivalries, and battlefield gossip.
documents.reasoning_trace: Document documents resistance: guard regiments stayed aristocratic, reforms applied unevenly between line/Landwehr and elite units; includes ancillary noise.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Between 1807 and 1815 Prussian reforms led by Scharnhorst created officer training institutions, introduced the Landwehr and merit-based promotion, and legally permitted capable lower ranks and qualified commoners to receive commissions. Consequently the noble share of officers fell from about 85% to 60% by 1815, middle-class officers rose to ~30% and commoner-origin officers to ~10%, though elite Guard regiments remained largely aristocratic.
